summary: A 1977 extension to FTP, called XRSQ and XRCP, for mailing the text of a message to several recipients at once on ITS FTP servers. It is far more efficient than sending the text again for each person.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of mailing the same letter to five people five times, send it once and name everyone who gets a copy.

questions: send mail to several recipients ftp
subtitle: Send one message to several recipients at once over FTP instead of sending it multiple times

tldr.problem: Sending the same message to multiple recipients using FTP requires transmitting the text again and again, wasting bandwidth and time, especially on ITS systems with central mail daemons.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 743 adds two new commands, XRSQ (to select a scheme) and XRCP (to specify recipients), with two different approaches: recipients-first (gather recipients then send text once) or text-first (send text once then specify recipients). The server announces which scheme it prefers, and both are valid.
tldr.outcome: Multi-recipient messaging became more efficient on supporting systems, though the extension remained limited to ITS implementations and did not become standard in FTP.

today: RFC 743 is an Unknown status experimental protocol from December 1977 for ITS FTP servers. It was implemented on MIT's ITS systems but did not become part of standard FTP.

sections.title: The Multi-recipient Problem
sections.content:
When a user of ITS FTP servers wants to send the same message to multiple recipients, the current practice requires sending the text again and again for each additional recipient. This wastes bandwidth and processing resources, especially inefficient for systems like ITS that hand off messages to a central mail daemon.

RFC 743 solves this by allowing a user to specify multiple recipients and send the message text once, avoiding redundant transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending the same email multiple times wasted network space. This extension sends it once and says who should all get it.

sections.title: Two Schemes: Recipients-First and Text-First
sections.content:
XRSQ selects which scheme to use. The recipients-first scheme (R) gathers all recipient names using XRCP commands, storing them in a list on the server, then sends the message text once with MAIL or MLFL. All recipients receive the same transmission in bulk.

The text-first scheme (T) sends the message text first with MAIL or MLFL, and then uses XRCP commands to specify each recipient. The server delivers the stored message individually to each recipient named. Neither scheme is optimal for all systems: R suits central mailers; T suits direct-delivery servers that return individual success/failure codes per recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Scheme R: write down everyone's name, then send the letter. Scheme T: send the letter, then write down the names. Different computers prefer different methods.

sections.title: Testing and Using the Extension
sections.content:
A user tests whether a server implements XRSQ by sending XRSQ with no argument, which must return 200 if supported. Sending XRSQ with a question mark asks the server to state its preferred scheme in a 215 reply. This negotiation allows clients to adapt to the server's capabilities.

Once a scheme is selected, MAIL or MLFL with no argument enters multi-recipient mode rather than failing. The stored recipients are flushed after the text transmission completes, resetting the state. This design avoids complicated state management while keeping the scheme selected for subsequent commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask the server if it supports the feature. Ask which way it likes best. Then specify recipients and send. The server forgets the list when done.
